title: Trump's Promise Accounting Faced Public Audit Pressure as AP Status Labels Hardened
description_short: Trump's Promise Accounting Faced Public Audit Pressure as AP Status Labels Hardened
description_medium: The Associated Press tracker used labels such as “kept,” “in progress,” and “complicated” to distinguish the status of Trump’s promises. The categories let readers compare individual commitments instead of treating them as a single completed record. They provide a public framework for checking broad claims, though they do not show that the tracker changed Trump’s messaging.
description_long: The Associated Press’s promise tracker grouped Donald Trump’s commitments under labels including “kept,” “in progress,” and “complicated.” Those categories separate a reported completion from a pledge still being pursued or facing obstacles, making it possible to review promises individually across policy areas. The format offers a more consistent comparison than treating a campaign’s promises as one undifferentiated total: each listed commitment can be examined on its own status and history. For readers following campaign pledges, the categories preserve a distinction between a promise reported as finished and one still incomplete or obstructed. The tracker functions as a public accounting tool, while the labels alone do not establish whether a policy succeeded or how much it affected people. A list of status labels can support comparison, but cannot on its own show that Trump faced meaningful public pressure or changed his messaging. The title’s claim about audit pressure requires evidence beyond the tracker’s categories.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Promise Accounting Faced Public Audit Pressure as AP Status Labels Hardened

notes: Needs context: the AP page returned HTTP 403; the packet establishes the tracker labels but not public response or a change in Trump’s messaging, as the title claims. Proposed correction: narrow the title to describe AP’s status categories unless evidence of public audit pressure is added.

title: Trump's Promise Accounting Became Easier for Critics to Audit at Scale
description_short: Trump's Promise Accounting Became Easier for Critics to Audit at Scale
description_medium: The Associated Press’s promise tracker places Trump’s commitments in a browsable list across policy areas. Readers can compare promises marked kept, in progress, or complicated instead of assessing each pledge through separate anecdotes. This structure supports a pattern-level review, although the tracker alone does not show that it changed Trump’s statements or policies.
description_long: The Associated Press’s promise tracker organizes Trump’s commitments across policy areas and assigns status labels such as kept, in progress, and complicated. Seeing those entries together lets readers compare the administration’s record across multiple pledges rather than rely on isolated examples. The tracker’s format gives critics and researchers a way to identify which promises are reported as fulfilled, which remain underway, and which face constraints. It turns the question of delivery into a set of specific items that can be checked over time. The project does not, by itself, establish how many readers used it, whether its status judgments changed Trump’s public messaging, or whether it affected policy outcomes. Its contribution is the organized comparison: promises that might otherwise be discussed one by one can be reviewed against the same visible categories. Any claim that this created broader political pressure would require evidence beyond the tracker’s existence.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Promise Accounting Became Easier for Critics to Audit at Scale
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Promise Accounting Became Easier for Critics to Audit at Scale

notes: The tracker supports a comparison across promises; the linked AP material does not document a resulting change in Trump’s messaging or policy.

title: Trump: Carl Icahn takes ownership of Trump Entertainment Resorts, Taj Mahal
description_short: Trump: Carl Icahn takes ownership of Trump Entertainment Resorts, Taj Mahal
description_medium: In February 2016, Carl Icahn took control of Trump Entertainment Resorts, bringing the Trump Taj Mahal out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy and making the company a subsidiary of Icahn Enterprises. Donald Trump gave up his remaining 10% stake. Icahn had committed $20 million in financing in 2014 as the casino faced closure.
description_long: In February 2016, Carl Icahn took control of Trump Entertainment Resorts and brought the Trump Taj Mahal out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The company became a subsidiary of Icahn Enterprises, and Donald Trump gave up his remaining 10% ownership stake. Icahn had previously committed $20 million in financing in 2014, shortly before the Atlantic City casino was scheduled to close. The transfer followed years of financial distress at the property and a restructuring process that had put the company in bankruptcy court. It marked a change in control: Icahn’s company assumed ownership while the Taj Mahal continued operating under its familiar name. The transaction ended Trump’s remaining ownership interest and placed the casino under Icahn Enterprises. It documents a corporate rescue and ownership change, but no broader result about casino workers or creditors is established by the ownership transfer itself.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Carl Icahn takes ownership of Trump Entertainment Resorts, Taj Mahal

title: Donald Trump and Dmitry Rybolovlev cross paths twice in a week
description_short: Donald Trump and Dmitry Rybolovlev cross paths twice in a week
description_medium: A 2016 timeline reports that Donald Trump’s campaign aircraft and Dmitry Rybolovlev’s plane were at the same airports in Las Vegas and Charlotte around October 30 and November 3, when Trump held rallies. It describes approximate timing and shared locations, but does not establish that the men met or communicated.
description_long: A timeline published after the 2016 campaign described two occasions when Donald Trump’s campaign jet and Dmitry Rybolovlev’s aircraft were reportedly at the same airports. The first overlap was in Las Vegas around October 30; the second was in Charlotte, North Carolina, around November 3, when Trump held rallies in both cities. The account says Rybolovlev did not explain his travel and presents the timing as a possible crossing of paths. That phrasing is stronger than the reported detail: planes arriving at one airport around the same time do not establish that their owners were present together, met, or exchanged messages. No meeting, conversation, or coordination is documented in the account. Its description characterizes the possible encounter as rumored rather than confirmed. What it does describe is a pair of approximate airport overlaps during campaign travel, a coincidence that cannot by itself establish contact or coordination.

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump and Dmitry Rybolovlev cross paths twice in a week
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump and Dmitry Rybolovlev cross paths twice in a week

notes: Needs context: the linked timeline reports approximate overlap between two aircraft, not a confirmed meeting between Trump and Rybolovlev. Proposed correction: retitle to describe the reported airport overlap or add evidence of an encounter; existing title asserts that the people crossed paths.

title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_medium: Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the NSA to install Michael Ellis as its general counsel in January 2021. The agency installed Ellis on January 19 and placed him on leave the next day as the presidential transition began. The supplied reports attribute the order to Miller, not to Trump personally.
description_long: In January 2021, Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the National Security Agency to install Michael Ellis as the agency’s general counsel. Ellis had served as counsel to Representative Devin Nunes and participated in the House Intelligence Committee’s review of the Trump-Ukraine matter. The NSA installed him on January 19, his first day in the role, and placed him on leave the following day during the presidential transition. The appointment placed a new general counsel inside a major intelligence agency at the end of the administration. Miller’s order was carried out on the eve of the transition, then Ellis was placed on leave as the administration changed. The source attributes the directive to the acting defense secretary and does not establish that Trump personally ordered it. The sequence also does not show that Ellis changed agency operations or affected a particular investigation.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
